name: Rotator Cuff Tendinopathy / Subacromial Pain
summary: Load-related rotator cuff pain, often aggravated by elevation and overhead activity; modern management emphasizes active rehabilitation rather than a purely mechanical 'impingement' model.

redFlags: Unexplained severe night pain or malignancy concerns
Acute traumatic weakness suggesting full-thickness tear
firstSteps: Education and temporary modification of provocative overhead volume
selfCare: Modify but do not completely avoid shoulder use

assess: Pain/weakness with resisted abduction or external rotation
Scapular movement impairment in some patients

tests.name: Painful Arc
tests.purpose: Assess pain during loaded/elevated shoulder range.
tests.positive: Concordant shoulder pain during a mid-range arc, commonly around 60–120°.

tests.name: Hawkins-Kennedy
tests.purpose: Provocative test for subacromial/rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain.

stages.label: Load Modification & Pain-Controlled Activation
do: Education and temporary modification of provocative overhead volume
dose: Isometric ER/abduction: 3–5 x 20–45 s at tolerable effort
moveOn: Able to load cuff without prolonged flare

stages.label: Resistance & Capacity
stages.goal: Increase rotator cuff and scapular strength/endurance.
when: Able to load cuff without prolonged flare
dose: Progress load when technique is good and symptoms settle by next day

stages.label: Overhead / Sport-Specific Return
stages.goal: Restore high-load and repetitive overhead capacity.
dose: Throwing/overhead volume increased gradually with recovery monitoring

logic: The main rehabilitation target is shoulder load capacity.
Pain with elevation does not automatically mean tendon damage is worsening.
Use manual therapy or taping only to make movement/exercise easier.
mechanism: Age-related tendon change with load sensitivity
classification: Partial-thickness cuff tear may exist on same continuum
investigations: Imaging is not routinely required for uncomplicated initial presentation.
Ultrasound/MRI may be considered for traumatic weakness, failed rehabilitation, suspected major tear or surgical planning.
manual: Glenohumeral, scapular, cervical or thoracic manual therapy may be used for short-term pain relief or mobility restriction.
Manual therapy should be paired with active rehabilitation.
Glenohumeral/thoracic mobilization when movement is limited
Soft-tissue treatment as a short-term adjunct
MWM when a painful movement improves immediately
Glenohumeral or thoracic mobilization can be used when movement is restricted.
MWM can be trialed if it immediately improves painful elevation.
Soft-tissue work may reduce short-term sensitivity; follow with loading.
modalities: Therapeutic ultrasound is not recommended for calcific or noncalcific rotator cuff tendinopathy in the 2025 CPG.
Shockwave may be considered for calcific tendinopathy, but not routinely for noncalcific tendinopathy.
Taping may provide short-term pain reduction when added to exercise.
TENS is optional for temporary pain.
dosing: Scaption or overhead raise: 2–3 sets × 8–15 reps.
Progress to overhead and task-specific load.
progression: Increase resistance when symptoms settle within 24 hours and technique remains good.
Progress from below-shoulder work to overhead, then speed and endurance.
Use work/sport demands to set the final stage.
mistakes: Calling every shoulder pain 'impingement' without differential screening
Keeping resistance too light to build capacity.
Assuming imaging abnormalities are the full cause of symptoms.
pearls: Manual therapy can help short-term symptoms but does not replace load-capacity rehabilitation.
education: Encourage modified use rather than complete rest.
Teach acceptable exercise pain and next-day monitoring.
escalation: Medical imaging/review for major traumatic weakness, persistent severe disability or failure after adequate rehabilitation

tests.name: Painful Arc
tests.purpose: Assess pain during loaded/elevated shoulder range.
tests.positive: Concordant shoulder pain during a mid-range arc, commonly around 60–120°.
procedure: Ask the patient to actively abduct/elevate the arm through full available range.
Note the angle and location of pain.
tests.interpretation: Supports subacromial/rotator-cuff-related pain but is not specific alone.

tests.name: Hawkins-Kennedy
tests.purpose: Provocative test for subacromial/rotator-cuff-related shoulder pain.
tests.patientPosition: Sitting or standing; shoulder and elbow at about 90° flexion.
tests.handPlacement: Support elbow with one hand and control wrist/forearm with the other.
procedure: Ask whether familiar shoulder pain is reproduced.
tests.interpretation: Supports rotator-cuff/subacromial pain as part of a clinical cluster.

tests.name: Jobe / Empty Can
tests.patientPosition: Standing or sitting; arms elevated in scapular plane around 90°.
procedure: Apply downward resistance while patient maintains elevation.
tests.interpretation: Supports supraspinatus/rotator cuff involvement; marked weakness after trauma warrants tear assessment.

story.headline: The shoulder that disliked shelves—but wasn't necessarily trapped
story.scene: A painter reaches overhead all week, then notices a familiar ache lifting a kettle to the top shelf. His friend says, 'Your tendon is being pinched by a bone, forever.' The shoulder deserves a better script.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'So there is no room inside my shoulder?' Therapist: 'We don't have to blame a tiny tunnel for every painful reach.'
story.clue: Gradual load-related shoulder pain and painful resisted elevation can fit rotator cuff-related pain. The old one-size-fits-all impingement explanation oversimplifies the problem.
story.twist: Painful tests can overlap across shoulder conditions. Trauma with sudden major weakness or marked loss of active elevation changes the referral pathway.
story.aha: The goal is not to 'create space' with magic hands; it is to restore tolerable load and useful movement.
story.patientTranslation: Your shoulder tendons may be sensitive to the amount of work they are doing. We'll adjust aggravating loads and build capacity gradually rather than permanently ban overhead tasks.
story.clinicianReasoning: Differentiate cuff-related pain from acute tear, cervical referral and serious pathology. Establish irritability and strength, then dose progressive cuff/scapular exercise and functional exposure; use hands-on care only as an adjunct.
story.rehabBridge: Settle painful overload → progressive resisted cuff and scapular work → overhead strength and confidence appropriate to the job.
story.question: Which plan best fits uncomplicated load-related rotator cuff pain?
options: Assume every painful arc confirms a torn tendon
Education plus progressive, symptom-guided exercise with adjuncts as indicated
story.explanation: Exercise and education are central to rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; individual tests and passive treatments alone are not definitive solutions.
